key_insight: The paper shows that a base model’s reasoning ability can be dramatically boosted by simple starting-token cues learned from training data. With the right cue, a plain base model can approach or match RL-trained performance on math and coding tasks.
problem_solved: It addresses the gap between base models and RL-trained models in reasoning performance, and explains why seemingly small response-prefix choices can strongly affect outcomes.
method: Analyze how specific initial tokens or short prefixes correlate with downstream reasoning behavior in training data.
Fix different starting-token cues at generation time and measure their effect on math and coding benchmarks.
Compare base-model performance under cueing against RL-trained counterparts to quantify how much of the gap can be closed by prompt prefix selection.
impact: This matters because it suggests some of the value attributed to RL training may be recoverable through simple, low-cost cueing strategies. Practitioners can potentially improve reasoning performance without additional training, using prompt design informed by data-driven token associations.
visual_elements: Before/after bar chart showing benchmark accuracy with and without specific cues.
Pipeline diagram linking training-data prefixes to response style and reasoning quality.
Side-by-side model comparison panel: base model vs RL-trained model vs cued base model.
Token-cue callouts highlighting example prefixes like ".\n\nOkay" and "Alright,".
paper_title: Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data
paper_authors: Sophie L. Wang, Amil Dravid, Rulin Shao, Kevin Farhat, Sewon Min
